new_statements.locator: Front matter, section 'Ibanị phonology and orthography', sub-section 'Tones', p. x (PDF page 11 of 103); phonology section begins p. viii
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (103 pp., Acrobat text layer, 'Microsoft Word - Ibani composite.doc', author Roger Blench, created 2005-04-25). extracted text of PDF page 11 (printed p. x) ends with the passage exactly as quoted: 'Tones / Ibanị has a relatively restricted tone-system, distinguishing High, Low and Downstep, like many Ịjọ and Igbo lects. The conventions are as follows; / low tone, unmarked / ´ high tone / ¯ downstepped high tone'. It sits in the editor's front-matter essay 'Notes on the Ibanị language' (signed Roger Blench), sub-section 'Ibanị phonology and orthography' (starts printed p. viii, PDF p. 9), which opens 'The principal description of Ibanị is in Fọmbọ (1975) a locally-published pedagogic…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ibani is described as a tone language with a small inventory of High, Low and downstepped High; every dictionary headword carries lexical tone (low unmarked, acute high, macron downstep), and syllabic nasals bear tone. The source says nothing about word stress or accent at all; there is no statement of stress position, of stress being absent, or of any interaction between tone and prominence.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The editor notes (p. i) that a full explanation of the phonology and orthography is still to be reconstructed from existing publications, and (p. viii) that the phonology is very similar to most Ijoid languages; the section is the editor's summary drawing on Fọmbọ 1975.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical/word-level tone on dictionary citation forms; no phrase-level or intonational information.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source describes Ịbanị (Bonny) proper, glottocode iban1261, from material collected at Finima-Bonny (Abe Brown ms.) and Fọmbọ 1975; it is the PHOIBLE source for Ibani. Wikipedia and Ethnologue treat Ibani as a dialect of Kalabari, but the Kalabari phonological literature (Harry 2003 JIPA; Harry 2004 CSLI) describes Kalabari proper (kala1381), not Ibani, and was not used here.

new_statements.quote: [p. 9] Um die Bezeichnung der Aussprache so genau wie möglich zu machen habe ich bei mehrsilbigen Wörtern den Akzent angegeben [...] [p. 52] Das Adjektiv oder Pronomen wird oft mit seinem nachfolgenden zweisilbigen Substantiv in der Aussprache zu einem Worte zusammengezogen, wobei das Substantiv wenn es auf der ersten Silbe akzentuirt war, den Ton verliert, das Adjectiv dagegen auf der letzten Silbe, statt auf der vorletzten betont wird, z. B. kálla tóbo — kallátobo; éri túbo — eritubo.
new_statements.translation: [p. 9] To make the indication of the pronunciation as exact as possible I have marked the accent on polysyllabic words [...] [p. 52] The adjective or pronoun is often contracted in pronunciation with its following disyllabic noun into one word, whereby the noun, if it was accented on the first syllable, loses its accent, while the adjective is stressed on the last syllable instead of the penultimate, e.g. kálla tóbo — kallátobo; éri túbo — eritubo.
new_statements.citation: Köler, Hermann. 1848. Einige Notizen über Bonny an der Küste von Guinea, seine Sprache und seine Bewohner, mit einem Glossarium. Göttingen: Dieterich. 196 pp.
new_statements.locator: Printed p. 9 (scan page 17), end of the introductory 'Vorwort' on the language; and printed p. 52 (scan page 60), in the 'Schlußbemerkungen' grammar notes that follow the Glossarium (pp. 48-53)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Both quoted passages re-read against the page images: printed p. 9, 4th paragraph: 'Um die Bezeichnung der Aussprache so genau wie möglich zu machen habe ich bei mehrsilbigen Wörtern den Akzent angegeben, ferner das scharfe s..') and..printed p. 52, mid-page: 'Das Adjektiv oder Pronomen wird oft mit seinem nachfolgenden zweisilbigen Substantiv in der Aussprache zu einem Worte zusammengezogen, wobei das Substantiv wenn es auf der ersten Silbe akzentuirt war, den Ton verliert, das Adjectiv dagegen auf der letzten Silbe, statt auf der vorletzten betont wird, z. B. kálla tóbo — kallátobo; éri túbo — eritubo.'). Verbatim apart from long s -> s, as the reader declared; the scanned files (pages/)…
new_statements.relation_note: Different type: Köler (1848) describes a per-word 'Akzent' with lexically variable position and says nothing about tone, whereas the catalog's statement of record (Blench 2005) treats Ịbanị as a High/Low/downstep tone language with no stress statement. The two are not really in conflict about the facts: Köler's acute marks are almost certainly the high tones of a pre-tonological ear (the words he marks on the second or final syllable are those Blench's dictionary and the Ijoid word list write with H there), and the p. 52 'loss' and 'shift' of accent in adjective-noun contraction looks like tonal sandhi in the compound, not stress movement. Köler gives no evidence for word stress as distinct…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Köler treats Bonny (Ịbanị) as a language with a word accent that he marks with an acute on every polysyllabic word of the glossary; he gives no placement rule, and the marked position varies from word to word (initial: kálla, tóbo, térra, szónna, áti, p. 10; second: inínne, eszánji, Ogúllo, Ebúnga, pp. 10-12; final: ngárrahně, ibingá, atarregá, pp. 10, 51-52). The p. 9 passage also says a final a is short 'even when the accent (Ton) rests on it'. He never mentions tone or pitch as a lexical category; his 'Akzent'/'Ton' is a single perceived prominence per word.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 52: in adjective/pronoun + disyllabic noun phrases pronounced as one word, the noun loses its (initial) accent and the adjective's accent moves from the penultimate to the final syllable (kálla tóbo > kallátobo; éri túbo > eritubo). Pp. 52-53 also describe vowel elision and consonant insertion at word junctions (kall' éhkwe for kálla ehkwe; ngá áhne > ngarráhne).
new_statements.identity_note: Köler's 'Bonny-Sprache' is the language of Bonny town (his glossary calls it 'Okólloma bibi', p. 53), which he explicitly distinguishes from Ibo, Brass (Nembe) and New Calabar (Kalabari, 'Umbógo bibi', p. 51) speech; this is Ịbanị (iban1261). The ÖNB copy read is the same 1848 Göttingen (Dieterich) printing as the listed HathiTrust/Google Books scans (title page, scan page 5).

readall_conflicts: Köler 1848 and Blench 2005 disagree in framing but not in substance. Köler marks a word 'Akzent' on every polysyllable, gives no rule for where it falls (initial, second and final syllables all occur in his glossary), and reports that in adjective+noun contractions the noun loses its accent and the adjective's accent moves to its last syllable; he never mentions tone. Blench 2005 (the existing statement) describes Ịbanị as a High/Low/downstep tone language and says nothing about stress. Read together, Köler's acutes are the high tones of a tone language transcribed by an 1848 observer, and his accent 'shift' is tonal sandhi; nothing in Köler supports a stress rule, so the catalog reading stays tone language, no stress statement. Ngulube 2011 could not be opened, so its tag 'likely states stress' is unverified.
